utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everybody. Good morning to the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, and the accused. Today we are to proceed with the testimony of Nelson Draper. Before he comes into the courtroom, I'm going to ask the registrar to gives some IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. 5D has submitted a list of documents to be tendered through witness Patrick van der Weijden. The list shall be assigned exhibit number IC 513. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Hakan Birger. The OTP list shall be given Exhibit number IC 514. 3D list shall be given Exhibit number IC 515, 4D list shall be given Exhibit number IC 516. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very well. We're not at all in a hurry. We have nearly two days ahead of us. As I reminded you yesterday, the Prosecution will have two hours, as scheduled. We've received from them all the documents they plan to put into evidence through the witness and, as to the Defence counsel, they, too, have two hours for their cross-examination. I don't know which documents they plan to prepare and present. So this is how the hearing is going to unfold. Please, Mr. Usher, bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. First of all, I want to check whether you can hear in your language my words as they're being translated. If so, please say yes, you understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, sir, state your surname, first name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Draper, first name Nelson, date of birth 15 April 1954.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Current occupation is truck driver, working in the oil patch where I live in Saskatchewan, Canada.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you had an opportunity to testify before a court of law as to the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia or is this the first time you're going to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please sit down. Since this is the first time you are going to testify, let me give you some explanations as to the way this hearing is going to take place. First you will have to answer questions put to you by the representatives of the OTP. I suppose you have met them yesterday or the day before yesterday, and they will ask questions of you. They will also submit documents to you. I suppose you have reviewed these documents with them before. Once this is done, the Defence counsel, they are on your left, there are many of them but rest assured there will only be one per accused who will put questions to you, and it may be that the accused themselves ask questions as part of what we call the cross-examination. As to the four Judges who are in front of you, as per rules, they can ask questions at any time, but it's been a while now. We prefer waiting until all parties have completed their examination in order to ask questions to clarify some of your answers or because we think that some important questions that should have been put to you did not get to be put. So it is then important in our eyes for -- in the interests of justice to ask you those questions. Try to provide clear answers, because, as you know, these are trial proceedings that are also kept -- and the record of which is kept in a transcript. So it's important for us to have your answers to the questions, because it's on the basis of your answers that we will make our final decision. If you do not understand a question, do not hesitate to ask the person asking you that question to reformulate it. If at any time you do not feel well, there -- again, ask us to have a break. We have a break anyway every 90 minutes. We break for 20 minutes for you to have a rest, on one hand, and on the other hand so that the tapes can be replaced. So this is what I wanted to tell you so that your testimony can take place in the best possible conditions for you and for all of the people present here in the courtroom. So this being said, I'm now giving the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to the Defence counsel and to everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Draper. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, I can sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I know that these proceedings will seem a little intimidating to you. I assure you that they're not and please feel relaxed, but it's important that you keep your voice up so that everybody hears you. So speak into the microphone if you will, please. Now, you told us that you were a driver, I think working in the private sector. I think previous to that you had worked in the public sector and were a member of the Canadian Armed Forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I joined the Canadian armed forces 30th November 1972, as a military policeman, and I stayed a military policeman throughout my career with the Canadian Armed Forces, and I retired approximately 20th of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And could you tell Your Honours what training as a military police you received during the course of your career within the Canadian Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Basically you went through the normal boot camp for the Canadian Armed Forces, and right after that I went to military police school to commence basic military police procedures, training, which dealt with ordinary traffic accidents, simple investigations, this type of procedures that were taught. Once that training has taken place we're posted to a business where you commence normal duties which could include security, ordinary policing duties. And as your career progressed you went back to the training school, which I did on numerous occasions, and you upgraded your police training to involve more intensive police techniques that involved interviews, interrogations, and this continued on. It's a continuing process right throughout your career. And accompanied by this you take a -- like, you upgrade your leadership training at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And by the year 1990, what was your rank within the Canadian Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: By this time I had reached a rank of a warrant officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I think warrant officer is a senior non-commissioned officer; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And with that rank, did your responsibilities increase?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. For a warrant officer, you're looking after subordinates that you instruct and look after, that there are reporting procedures and then you report to a higher command.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what was the largest number of subordinates that you were in charge of and looked after?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Approximate -- approximately 30 at one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were these other military police officers?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, these would be other military police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, in the course of your career, did you serve abroad?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I served abroad on temporary duty to Bosnia for six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you went to Bosnia and how long you spent there?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I went to Bosnia with the former United Nations Military Police Platoon to look after the Bosnia-Herzegovina area, with the exception of Sarajevo. There were six of us from Canada that came over to start it up. We were supposed to have a contingent of, I think, between 30 and 50 military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could you just stop there. What year was this, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: This would be 1993. I think we left -- left Canada and arrived in Zagreb on the 8th of October, 1993, and then on the 10th of October, 1993, we made our way to Kiseljak, Bosnia-Herzegovina, where the BH command was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us in very brief, general terms what your duties were in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: The duties in Kiseljak would be providing United Nations police service to the country, which we dealt with anything that involved a peacekeeping unit with -- with the civilian side of the house or -- whereas their own units have their own regimental police that deal with events happening in their own units. If it involved any civilian aspect, like a traffic accident, that's where the United Nations military police would come into being to look after investigations of that type. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Sorry, continue. Can you tell us what was the military police chain of command for your unit for the period you were serving there?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: These military police would report to me, and I would report to Captain Gale, who was the platoon commander, and Captain Gale would report to the command provost marshall, who was at the time Major Dongor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did your duties include criminal investigations?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, they would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Sometime in October 1993, can you receive orders from your superior regarding an investigation of alleged crimes committed in a location called Stupni Do outside the town of Vares?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It would have been on the evening of the 26th of October, 1993, where Lieutenant Gale approached me and tasked me with investigating what he termed a massacre that had occurred at the village of Stupni Do in which civilians were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you say "massacre." Were you given much of a briefing or overview what was alleged -- as to what was alleged to have occurred?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: It was -- if memory serves, it was -- they were saying it was an HVO-led attack that had occurred on the village and that civilians were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know who was the -- who was living in the village at the time? What predominant faction was living there, what predominant ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: BiH. It was my understanding it was a BiH pocket of mainly Muslims that were in a Croat-controlled pocket, or HVO-controlled pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, who was to be the lead investigator for the purpose of this investigation?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I was assigned the lead investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us, when did you arrive to Stupni Do and who, if anybody, travelled with you?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: BH command put together a convoy proceed Stupni Do which consisted of BH command authorities, some legal people, press people, and my MP team, and we left Kiseljak and proceeded towards Stupni Do stopping at the town of Dabravine on the way there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: What was the purpose of this stop in Dabravine?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: When I -- when we arrived there I was able to speak to a BiH official who had told me that there was numerous survivors of Stupni Do in that town. So I had teed up with them to try to get me some names so that once I come back from looking after or investigating the site that I would be able to interview some of the witnesses. Once that was done, we proceeded on to Stupni Do, arriving just before noon hour on the 27th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the condition of the village when you arrived on the 27th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah. On arrival, as we were coming in sight of the village, you could tell that most of the village had been destroyed, burnt. You could see burn, scorch marks on most of the houses. Most of the roofs were gone, collapsed in on themselves. Exiting the vehicle you could smell burnt -- the smell of burnt -- there was like a -- like a garbage dump was that distinct smell of burnt flesh.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you notice anything else?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Dead animals, garbage all -- well, debris all the other the place, expended ammunition casings, grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you remember -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you remember when you arrived if there were any residents living in the village?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: No. There were no residents at the time. The -- the village was -- had been -- at the time was being secured by BritBat company providing security at the village at the time, the commander of which was Major Roy Hunter, I believe it was, who had -- I had spoken to about what was going on in the village at the time and dealing with security, and I had -- I knew the intentions were to let the press -- I think General Ramsay wanted to have the press there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: General Ramsay was the senior commander with --

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, he was the senior commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: With UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You arrived on the 27th. This was three days after the alleged massacre in Stupni Do. Do you know if anybody else, any other groupings, UNPROFOR or otherwise, had already visited the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. When I converse with Major Hunter, he had said he relieved NordBat, I believe it was that morning, and they had been in there at that time, and they relieved them. So you had two -- two different groups that had already been through this at the time searching the village. And considering -- considering this, I -- I had no reservations per se to allow the press people to film the village because I knew the -- it wasn't really a secure crime scene because of the -- all the troops that had been rummaging around the village. So my main concern was just to have Major Roy's people keep an eye on the press to make sure they didn't tamper with anything, pick stuff up, or otherwise disturb the scene any more than it was already disturbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And so when you arrived there and you met Major Hunter, what did you and your team, what was the first thing that you and your team did when you arrived there in furtherance of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I had Major Hunter who had already located -- knew where locations where a lot of the bodies were, and so I asked him to show myself and my team to all the body locations so I could have a quick overview of what -- where they were, and he did this, and we were followed by the press people. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many bodies you viewed?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Total was 16. They were at various locations in the -- in the village itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you describe the condition of these bodies? Were they identifiable when you first saw them?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Not all of them. There was around seven of them that you could identify, and then the rest were just burnt too far to even tell if they were female or male, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, as lead investigator, did you assign specific tasks to your team members?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had assigned master corporal Scott McKee with the crime scene processing because he had an AV course, which in Canada is a military police course that dealt with crime scene processing on how to handle evidence, that type of thing. So he went through training just specifically for that type of thing. So him having that qualification I told him he would be processing the crime scenes, and I think it was Staff Sergeant Verne I had detailed to be the evidence custodian, to look after any evidence that they may have picked -- we may have picked up at the time while we were there, and had one other individual, I think Sergeant Platteau, P-l-a-t-t-e-a-u, I believe. He was to help in any other way, in case we needed anyone like a -- i.e., will help with witnesses and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: No, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were all of these soldiers members of the Canadian contingent?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: No. The only Canadian that I had at the time was Master Corporal McKee. I didn't have room to bring anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you might have answered this already, but can you tell us what your priorities were and what tasks, specific tasks your team undertook, and what your priorities were on this first day?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: The main priorities on this day was to process the crime scene as fast as we could because I knew we were on a limited time-frame because the units that were guarding the village for us had other escort duties, other duties in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This wasn't part of their duties. It was something they were doing other than their duties, and they had to go back to those duties. So that being said, I wanted to get as much done before we got pulled out of there as we could. So I instructed Master Corporal McKee where to start with the -- the crime scenes where we could identify the victims first and then each place where there was a body type -- or bodies would be a crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you have your team search the area for physical and material evidence related to the incident?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. That would be mainly on -- under Master Corporal McKee's responsibilities as he was processing the crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what would happen to any evidence that they discovered?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: The evidence they discovered would have been handed over, well, bagged and tagged type thing, would have been picked up and tagged and then given to staff sergeant Verne who would keep a log of it and secure it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: On this first day was your team accompanied by a photographer?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: We didn't have a photographer available in our Military Police Platoon at the -- well, we never had any equipment whatsoever. There was no crime processing equipment that we had or anything, so we eventually found a BritBat photographer that happened to be on scene, then used his services.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of that photographer?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Pettersen, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And how long did Mr. Pettersen remain with you until?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I assigned him with Master Corporal McKee, so I don't know if he was there both days or just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And his function was to take photographs of the crime scene, of the remains and the bodies, I assume?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Exactly. Anything and everything that related to the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Was anybody designated to prepare sketches of the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. Staff sergeant Verne the evidence custodian also at the same time was preparing a hand-drawn sketch of the scene, of the town that -- the main part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, given the stated -- the limitations of your time and the deadlines, did your team manage to finish on that first day? Did they manage to finish the crime scene inspections on the first day?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: No. We had arrived there around noon, and at close to 4.00 or shortly after 4.00 it was getting dark, so we had to pack it in. We had no additional lighting or anything. So at that time we made our way to NordBat, who had a small base nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you meet -- did you meet representatives of the NordBat unit, and did you speak to them about the Stupni Do massacre?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah. I spoke to several of them there. Major Ekhard [sic] who was the deputy commander, I believe, and a couple of the other regimental military police who were there at the time. I spoke to them and got a little bit more information of what had gone on at Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what kind of information did they -- did they give to you as to what had happened at Stupni Do or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: They related that the day of the attack and then the next day they knew the attack was going on at Stupni Do, and the HVO would not let them pass to go into the village. On the -- they tried again on the 24th. They still didn't -- still couldn't get in. And on the 25th they finally were able to make it into the village. I also spoke to another officer that had gone to -- on the 24th, I believe, in the -- he went to his observation post at -- nearby at -- near the town of Dastansko. They had observation post there, and he was saying that at 10.00 that day when he went there he could hear some motors and small-arms fire, and later that evening he could also see that the sky above Stupni Do was just red from fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not any of these NordBat officers had carried out any interviews with anybody related to what had happened in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: One of the -- Major -- Ekhard -- Ekberg?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Ekberg.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Ekberg had talked to a couple of women who said they had been raped, that the attacking force had killed indiscriminately civilians without -- actually, but rape, theft.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did they mention anything else other than the killings?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Well, other than -- you know, that they burnt everything. They would be able to give you more information. I'd probably have to refer to something, some notes or -- because I got too much in my mind. I don't know if I'm skipping ahead of myself or -- or --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: We'll come back --

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: But generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: We'll come back to it in a moment.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Rape, killings, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just interrupt. As far as we're concerned in the Stojic Defence, we have -- we would have no objection to the witness referring to notes of his investigation. It would be standard in the case of a police officer and might save some time if -- so Mr. Flynn should please feel free to do that, as far as we're concerned, if that would help.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm very happy to hear that, Your Honours, and I'm grateful to the members of the Defence team for mentioning that. And I will ask -- I will ask Mr. Draper to refer to his notes in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Just going back to the -- the crime-scene investigations, did your team return on the second day to Stupni Do, on the day after?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. They had to return to finish off the crime scene processing, which they eventually did after that second day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were you with the team on this day?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Not entirely, no. The -- the -- Master Corporal McKee was looking after everything the second day at the village itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, during these two days of examinations, did you -- do you know whether or not the team availed the use of a medical examiner or a medical officer to examine the bodies?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah. That second day a medical officer accompanied Master Corporal McKee. So -- and they went to each body that was there and did a quick assessment of the body, the results of -- of which later on in a debriefing with him indicated that most had been shot. Some appeared to have what was, I believe, to be stab wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you know were any weapons found on or near any of the bodies or remains?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: For the most part, no. One body had some live shells, and I believe a grenade or two near the body. And this body had the -- the body had most of the clothes burnt off. It had combat boots, so we had assumed that it was either a HVO or a BiH soldier or a defender. We weren't quite sure at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you -- was your team able to finish the crime scene examinations on the second day?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you know how many crime scenes were examined in total by your team on these two days?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Seven. Seven, you know, in different parts of -- different areas where the main location of the bodies were. They were marked down on the map that Staff Sergeant Verne had completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I can just jump ahead a little for a moment. Did you during the course of your investigations prepare written reports for your superiors?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I -- I submitted a total of four of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And on the 15th of November -- or did you prepare a report dated the 15th of November, a substantive interim report listing the seven crime scenes?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And that stated other information as well as what was found on the crime scenes?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher I wonder if I may at this stage introduce Exhibit number 06978. You'll find it at the start of the second book, Mr. Draper. And if you could turn the page to the first -- to the fourth page with ERN number 00053356. Is this the report that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you could go later and go to page 0053385. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: There are two signatures on that page. Is that your signature in the middle of the page and that have your superior --

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: -- following?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: First signature is myself. Second signature is my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you could go farther to page 00553391 you will find a map.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, which is the map that staff sergeant Verne drew.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So when I asked you about whether there were sketch maps prepared, is this the map that was prepared by members of your team?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And does this map basically indicate where the bodies were -- the remains and bodies were located?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, if you turn to page 00053359 of the same report. It's at the start almost. It's a couple of pages beyond the start.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: From paragraph 2 until paragraph 4, do you set out what you actually found at the crime scenes, the various -- the seven crime scenes that you inspected?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. These is where it describes each crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And was that report prepared based on your notes solely or on the combination of your notes and those of your team members?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: It was a combination of my notes and the team members.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And could you tell the trial panel very briefly -- I don't want you to read the report, but could you tell them -- go through crime scene 1 to crime scene 7 the basics of what you found?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Well, crime scene was a house there. In the -- the lower floor was three dead women in a trap door leading to a lower area, a basement area, like a root cellar or something. And outside the back was one body, and then the other bodies were in the upper level of that house, burnt beyond recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And there were three female bodies is that correct, which you lettered A, B, and C on the map?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, three female bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And these were later found -- identified as Nevzeta Likic, Hatidza Likic, and Medina Likic?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Look at the second part of that first crime scene report. Is it correct to say that the badly burnt body that was found was believed to be that of Adis Likic?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. This is the one I had mentioned -- sorry, say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is the body -- was that body believed to be the body of Adis Likic?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Oh, the one outside the house in scene 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at subparagraph 2 of scene 1.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Right. Right. This is Adis Likic. This is the one that we at first for a good part thought might be female and later once I interviewed his mother found out it was a male.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And his body was letter D on the map, the sketch map. It's on the first line.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the first part of the crime scene 1 there were three badly burned bodies, E, F, and G, of which were marked on the map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: The mother and two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: These were later -- were they -- were they established as being Merima Likic, Mebrura Likic, and Vahidin Likic, or was it just a belief?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: This was confirmed later on through witness interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That's how we determined who was -- who was -- was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you move now to scene 2 and just briefly tell me what was found there.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah. Scene 2 was the gentleman that I had mentioned earlier that had most of his clothing burnt off, with the exception of the combat boots, and there was some ammunition and a grenade or two I found around his body.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And he was -- he was later -- that was -- that body was later believed to be the body of Samir Likic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, at scene 3 what did you find?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Scene 3 was found between two dwelling -- like in a walkway, and we later identified him as - pronunciation - Salih Likic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Salih Likic?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Salih Likic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And scene 4?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Scene 4 remains -- just have a look here. Yeah. He was in front of a house, and he was severely charred. It was hard -- hard to say. The medical opinion, I remember, was they weren't sure if the body was a person or an animal, but some of the medical -- other medical people thought it was probably a person. So that's how we treated it. There was some doubt, so we just treated it as a human.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you ever get confirmation that it was a human afterwards?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I believe -- I can't recall. From the autopsy reports that I got later on I'm sure it was confirmed as a human. I can't quite say 100 per cent sure though.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: But, yeah, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And this body was letter J on your sketch map?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, scene 5. How many bodies did you find on scene 5?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Scene 5 there was four bodies. This was located on the -- the -- near the upper part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: And they were all pretty well burnt beyond recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And they were marked as K, L, M, and N on your sketch map?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Quite correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Later we identified them as -- well, as they're listed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You later -- for the record you later think you identified them as Edin Mahmutovic?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Rasida Likic.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Rifet Likic.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And Mehmet Likic?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now at scene 6, what did you find?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Scene 6 was the body of a man located near the same area, across the street, I think, lying on his back with a charred piece of lumber across his legs. He was later identified as Abdulah Likic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And moving on then to scene 7?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: And scene 7 was just a little bit outside a hill in just a little bit of a wooded area was an elderly gentleman that later returned -- we found out was the mayor's dad, Zejnil Mahmutovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Zejnil Mahmutovic?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Mahmutovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And this was a total seven crime scenes that your team had examined; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Apart from having photographs taken did you -- did your team through any other medium record the investigations?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: The second day we -- we were able to get a video camera, and so as the team went through, this was a -- they filmed the different crime scene areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And when was this taken and by whom?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: This would have been taken the next --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You arrived --

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: The 28th. The 28th. And it was taken by one of the members of -- I believe Sergeant Jim Steward who had come up that day, I think, because he brought the video camera with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, did you have an opportunity during your first few days of your investigations to interview any of the Stupni Do inhabitants or survivors? And I don't want you to mention any names at the moment.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us when this was?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: On the 29th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And without giving their -- their names to us at this point, can you tell us in general terms what they told you had happened in Stupni Do and who had taken part in the attack?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: The attack happened on the 23rd, the morning of the 23rd around 8.00 and continued throughout the day, petering out at around 4.30 that afternoon. The -- there were civilians lying out -- outside their houses shot, some women taken in the houses and raped, and they were saying that they were HVO that had -- had done this. And must having their valuables taken from them, their jewellery they were wearing or money that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Of course you mentioned when you arrived in the village seeing all the burned houses. Was there any mention of burnings and arson?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah. They were setting fires to all of their houses and taking the bodies of the people that they had killed and throwing them into the houses as they burnt to burn them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, did the witnesses identify who the attackers were, and did they give any descriptions of how they were dressed, weapons they were carrying or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: The -- they mentioned that they were HVO. They were wearing camouflage uniforms. Some were dressed in black, wearing flak jackets and white ribbons. Mostly white ribbons tied to their epaulettes, cammed-up faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: What did you say about faces?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Cammed. Disguised their faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Painted, camouflage?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: To blend in with the forest or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did any of the witnesses indicate that they had recognised any of those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Not at this time, I don't believe none of them were recognisable. They weren't soldiers that they recognised from -- locally, local soldiers. They all seemed foreign soldiers to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And these initial witnesses that you interviewed, did they indicate from what faction the soldiers had come, from which army?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Well, eventually a lot of the witnesses said they were from -- that the Kiseljak area, brought in from the Kiseljak area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But which army?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, I think at this point, Your Honours, I would have to ask to go into private session because I'm going to ask the witness something about one of the protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, private session, please. 21 [Private session] (readcted)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Draper, on the basis of your early discussions with the NordBat UNPROFOR forces and those few local witnesses that you initially interviewed, did you form any opinion as to who the perpetrators were?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: What their crimes had been, committed?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah. Based on my observations in the village myself and the interviews I had conducted up to that time there -- there was no doubt in my mind that -- like -- I don't know if the term "massacre "is appropriate, but killings of innocent people definitely take place, and it appeared that the HVO were the responsible party.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you learn from where the HVO forces had come from that had committed the attack?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. Eventually through the interviews I learnt that they had come from the Kiseljak area at different groups, one being the Apostoli, and the other one being the Maturice. I don't know if I have my pronunciation right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Have you heard the name Maturice? Does that ring a bell with you?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That was the one. That's the one, and the other --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Have you heard Apostoli?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Apostoli, yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you get any information as to who the commander was at the time this attack took place? And I know it's difficult for you to pronounce names.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I think Major Ramsay was -- at the time had mentioned Ivija Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Ivica?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Does the name Ivica Rajic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you or your team make any efforts to contact the HVO authorities for assistance with your investigation once you learned that it was the HVO, for fact that it was the HVO who had been involved?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. Once I got back to my unit, one of the first things I had done was make up a memo and sent it up the chain of command to the legal to get ahold of the HVO and let them know I wanted to talk to anyone involved in the attack on Stupni Do because I was doing the investigation and wanted to -- as much information as I could get on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were you aware personally at that time whether any assurances had already been given by anyone in the political or military hierarchy of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Not at the time. Not from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. So following the initial interviews that you held in the first few days after your investigation, did you carry out many further interviews with survivors and inhabitants of Stupni Do or other UNPROFOR forces?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. For my -- the rest of my tour there, when time would permit and circumstances would permit, I continued that investigation, trying to interview people involved with this attack until my tour ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us briefly how these interviews generally were conducted?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Usually what happened is once I located the subject, where they were, I would go, interview them at that location either it being, you know, in a school, their home, in a local public office, NordBat itself. I interviewed people there. So wherever the location permitted, that's where we did the interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were these interviews conducted by your members of your team in addition to yourself?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. All of my team from Canada were senior military policemen, so they had appropriate interview skills, and I used that to my advantage. So whenever we were able to go, I made sure I brought another team so we can do simultaneous interviews, get as many done as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you obtain written statements from the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Well, I tried. Most witnesses didn't want to provide written statements, but I eventually got hold of video equipment, and I used that quite -- most of them allowed me to videotape their interviews, and it was done in a normal police procedure where at the beginning of the interview we would identify them and make sure the information they gave was voluntary and not something that someone else said, something that they saw regarding the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us how many such interviews were conducted and over what period?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: From late October right -- I think last one was in March. Around -- around 50 thereabouts, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And where were these interviews conducted by and large?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Mostly wherever the people were located. If they happened to be -- near the beginning a lot of the interviews were done in Dabravine. And then once BA -- BiH took over the Vares area many of them moved back to Vares, and we did interviews there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you remember -- did you give a statement to the ICTY between the 20th and 23rd of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. They -- a couple of their members came over to Canada, and I met them in Toronto and provided them with a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And in that statement, is it correct to say that you listed many of -- the names of many of those interviewed by your team and the dates of the interviews?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. Mainly, though, my -- my interviews that I personally had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you stand by at that statement today?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, time won't allow us to go through all of the statements which you mention in your statement and those people you interviewed, but I just want to ask you about some of those interviewed. Do you remember, did you interview a person by the name of Suada Likic?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: She was one of the ones I interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And was -- was Suada Likic in the village of Stupni Do when the attack occurred?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you remember what she told you?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you mind if I briefly look at the notes just to make sure I don't get her confused with someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I'm sure I know which one it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm unable to give you a reference for this one. I thought you might have had the information.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah, I have it in my personal notebook. If I can refer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Murphy, do you also agree to the use of the personal notebook?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have no -- yes, Your Honour. We have no -- I think it's quite standard in the case of a police officer that he should be allowed to refer to notes, and I think Mr. Flynn would also agree that if it should become necessary for the purposes of cross-examination the Defence would be entitled to inspect any portions of the notes he may refer to. I don't say that will be necessary but it would follow from the normal practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I think for the sake of clarification, when you say -- or when you refer to your notebook, are these notes which you took during the course of the interviews?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Or shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: It would be right in the time frame, within that same day or within a few days after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you use those notes for the purposes of compiling the various reports, the substantive reports that you subsequently delivered to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Exactly. If you wish it, if it's more convenient, we can just use the report paragraph where I had interviewed the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, whichever --

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: It's going to be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Whichever is easier for you. If you could tell us which -- what Suada Likic told you happened.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Okay. So I interviewed her on -- yeah. I went to Vares on the 26th of Jan 1994, and I went to a building where there was an apartment complex, and there I was introduced to -- how do you pronounce her first name?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Suada.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Suada Likic, born in 1974 in Vares. So I did the normal interview with her, and she confirmed general events of that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did she mention the course -- during the course of her interview, having escaped, meeting a group of people in the forest?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, once the attack had finished and they finally escaped to the forest, she mentions at one point she had -- yeah. They had found -- there were 80 or 90 other villagers that they met, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did she mention -- did she mention meet lady who had been shot?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. Mufija Likic. I'm just seeing if I can see it here, but I remember her saying she had meet -- met --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mufida Likic, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. Mufida Likic. Oh, here we go. The group had many wounded, for -- one which was a girl who had -- who was shot in the leg, Mufida Likic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now did you also interview a lady by the name of Ferida Likic?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, just after I interviewed Ferida Likic, and that was on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I think at this stage we may need to go back into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, during the course of the various interviews that you conducted over the period that you stated, did you notice any major discrepancies or inconsistencies between the statements of the various witnesses?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Here and there I noticed little discrepancies, but with all the interviews I did, it provided a general overall view that was consistent with everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you get any information during this period of time whether or not the defendant -- the village had been defended on this day?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There -- there was approximately 36 BiH -- I guess they were BiH defenders that manned like trenches in different areas around the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, when you say BiH, were they described by the witnesses as BiH or --

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: No. Like they're village members. A lot of them would be -- I don't think they were -- I can't say for sure they were, you know, regular soldiers, you know, marksman-type like myself. The ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So they were villagers.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. Like most of them lived in that town.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at the end of March 1994, did you prepare another substantive report which turned out to be your last --

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: -- based on your investigations up to that date?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, before doing so, had you received any positive response from the HVO authorities to your earlier requests for assistance with your investigation that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: No. The memo I had originally sent to legal to try and go through proper channels to get to interview anyone involved in the attack didn't meet with any positive results for me, so I think it was in March that I tried getting an interpreter in Kiseljak to go direct to the HVO liaison officer to get me set up to interview Radic or --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Rajic, or a member -- you know, the commander of the - what do you call them? - Maturice, or anybody who was involved in the attack, but that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: What response did you get to that?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That was no -- didn't get a positive result on that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you told anything about Mr. Rajic at that particular time? Was he still in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I just -- I believe he -- they were just saying he wasn't available. And then for the commander of the other group, he had been wounded, was over in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Which other commander are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: It was the commander of either the -- one of the groups I had mentioned earlier, the Apostoli or --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Was this a commander below Mr. Rajic?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe -- yes, mm-hmm, because Rajic was the overall commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the upshot of all of this, did you actually get any cooperation, and were you able to interview anybody at all from any of the HVO units that had taken place -- that had taken part in the events in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, did you prepare -- did you prepare a written report dated the 26th of March, 1994, updating your earlier reports?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I think this was the last report that we mentioned?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And on the basis of your interviews and observations and notes and investigations had to that date, can you tell me how many deaths were attributed to the attack in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Total from all the interviews it turned out to be -- it turned out to be 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were their 38 bodies recovered from the crime scene by UNPROFOR or your investigative team?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: No. Only the 16 were recovered there. The rest were buried amongst the debris.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not there were any medical examinations or autopsies performed on those bodies recovered from either by UNPROFOR or BiH authorities outside the examinations carried out by the officer on the 28th of October.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes apparently the bodies went to the Visoko mortuary where autopsies were performed on the 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And who was it who performed those autopsies?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I believe it was the coroner at that mortuary. At one point we were able to obtain copies of them, which I believe I attached to one of my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And did you also manage to obtain video footage of the autopsies?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Right. I found out that they had conducted video footage, and I was able to obtain a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, at this stage I'd like you to turn in the second booklet to Exhibit 8121, 08121. It's halfway into the booklet.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Page number again?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: If you look at the tab firstly, 08121.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: What tab was this -- the four-digit tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The four-digit tab on the edge?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: What was it again you said?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Mine are all six digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The second booklet, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: 8121. And page?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, just look at the first page firstly. This is a letter dated the 28th of March. Please find here military police report for your information. And if you look at the following pages, is this a report prepared by you dated the 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Dated 26th of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Date the 26th of March. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, this is my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you turn to page 43 on that report, which is ERN number R0048851.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is that your signature and again the signature of your superior, Lieutenant Gale?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you see at the bottom of the page you annex a number of documents. The first document is Annex A. And if you turn over the page to page ER R0048852, you have a list of deceased.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Correct. That's a list of deceased from Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the total of this list is 38?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell us how this list was compiled?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: This was a list on the first day that we went to Stupni Do when I stopped off at Dabravine, and I spoke to that official and I had asked him to try and get me a list of villagers from Stupni Do. He provided shortly thereafter a lot of surviving members and a list of deceased members. That were -- where this list came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And this list contains the father's name of the deceased and the date of birth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you later learn that the date of births for some of the deceased mightn't correspond to their actual date of birth?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, could you turn to page 8 -- R -- R0048862. Which on e-court is 8815, 48 and 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: It's 8862; if you look for 8862.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: 8862, annex G to my report, interview dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: This is annex G?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: At the top. And interviews dates. Is this a list of those people who were interviewed by you during the period October to March?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Mainly of -- most of them are the villagers. There's a couple other ones like -- but mainly villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, could you go back to Annex F, please, which is on page 8861. This is another map.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, according to the annex, this should have contained photographs of the crime scenes, but in fact it contains a map. Are you able to explain that? Annex F, 8861.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Annex F.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you have the page?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah, I have it. Photographs depicting different massacre scenes. No. That should be -- that's a topographical map of Stupni Do, not photographs, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And there are seven -- the number 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 are marked on the map. Do these represent the crime scenes?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, lastly, could you turn Annex I, which is on page 8876.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: 48867 you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: No, 48876. Keep going. I think you have it.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Annex I?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: This is a, copy topographical map also, and on this map is marked deceased and various numbers. Can you tell us what this map is?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: This is the a copy of the same topographical map, and what I had done is mark the deceased's body locations according to the list of deceased that we had -- you had previously mentioned, 1 to 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So is it correct to say that this map should be read in conjunction with Annex A, which lists the numbers of the deceased?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Numbers of the deceased. Right. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, did you also around the same time prepare a briefing video to include in the results of your investigations including clips from autopsy examinations by BiH authorities and a small clip showing the damage to Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Right, I did. I went to Zagreb to do that video.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: At this stage, Your Honours, I would be asking to show the video, but I am aware that we have reached the break and perhaps Your Honours may deem it appropriate to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're going to take a break and then we'll have a look at the video. It's 10.30. We're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before watching the video, let me raise a technical issue. The interpreters have asked that they not be obliged to translate the video because on the screen there will be subtitles. I don't know what there is to see on that video. If someone speaks in English, for example, it's perfectly natural that what is being said in English should be translated into B/C/S. We want the public to be able to understand what is going on. If something is written in English and it's not interpreted, the people outside of this courtroom won't understand what's going on. Mr. Flynn, what is the problem? We have here the -- in our documents the transcript of what is said, but the public sitting outside of this courtroom does not have this document. So if they see a video, if they watch a video without being aware of the translation, that might cause a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, Your Honour. Firstly, let me tell you that what Your Honours will see are an extract from video Exhibit 06 -- 06318, which contains some sound and which will have the transcript appended to it during the course of the video. You will also see a video -- extract from a video 06321 which will have some sound, but the sound -- the sound -- it will just be sounds of machines. The actual speaking is blocked out. So when you're watching the first video, as you're watching it the transcript certainly will appear on English underneath. I'm not aware that it would appear also in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but my question is the following: What about the person listening to us or the person watching these proceedings who can only speak B/C/S? Would that person be able to understand what is being said in this video? That's the problem. Because if I look at 6318, if I have the transcript in English and if I also have the translation in B/C/S, as we all do here, that's fine, but outside of this courtroom those watching us do not have these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wouldn't it be possible for the interpreters to translate the subtitles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll ask the interpreters to do their best and then we'll see how it works. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry to jump up and interrupt.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt my colleague but my understanding is the booths have been provided with a B/C/S transcript of this videotape, so perhaps I've missed something along the way, but normally when there are transcripts, including in B/C/S, those are provided to the language booths. So I'm a bit at a loss as to why they simply couldn't read the transcript that's been provided to them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note there has never been any problem with -- with the interpreters doing the interpreting of the video. We were just wondering if we need to read the English despite the subtitles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We'll ask the interpreters to translate the subtitles. Okay. You can start the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I should say to you before I do -- before we do, Your Honours, that what you have in writing in front of you is a transcript of this complete exhibit, but I prepared a -- an excerpt from the exhibit because it would have taken us an hour to see the whole exhibit, and so you have a transcript and not all of this transcript will be read throughout the -- will appear in the video. So it will not be sufficient for the translators to read directly from the transcript, but the relevant portion of the transcript will appear with the video in English and I think they will be able to read from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes the first extract of the video. I have a very short video extract from video exhibit 06321, which is by the BBC and which I wanted you to see because it shows a clearer picture of scene 1, the scene in the basement, than the previous one did because it was a little bit dark. If you can run it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And that's merely the scene that I wanted you to see because you couldn't see it in the earlier video. We also have a compilation of the video taken during the autopsies performed by the BiH authorities. I don't propose we go through every single one of them, but what I'll ask Ms. Winner to do is to click on each one and we'll examine for a few seconds and move on. It shouldn't take any more than one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And that concludes the video exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mr. Draper, were you watching those?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you recognise the scenes depicted in the videos?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. They were the scenes at Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you visit them during the course of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: The scenes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the soldiers seen in the video are part -- are they part of your team, your investigation team?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. They are a part of my MP platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do the videos accurately reflect what was found at the start of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You saw the second scene on the first video which your team took. It took -- it was a photograph of what they described as what was believed to be a BiH soldier.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Was this person indeed a BiH soldier or was he found to be a civilian?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: He was a village defender.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your testimony this morning earlier, you mentioned that you had obtained the services of a photographer, Mr. Pettersen?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did he ultimately deliver the photos to you on your team?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Negatives, the negatives of the photos that he took.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: If you could just keep your voice up. And do you remember if there were many photos?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, there is quite a number of them. The total number I can't recall, but there was quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did all the photos relate to Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were the negatives delivered to you personally or to one of your team members?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: One of my team members.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know if at the same time Mr. Pettersen delivered a photographic log, a map of what was contained in the photographs?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah. I believe one -- what it came in, I probably didn't see it because it would have been entered right into the evidence at the time, but -- I can't physically say that I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'd like you just to have a look at Exhibit number 06099 for me. That's in the first book, the one with the -- the one with the table on the front of it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you turn to the first page you'll see "Photo Log," and it's reference number BSP 1, photographer B. Pettersen, and on the left-hand column he has negative numbers 1 to 10.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Sorry, can you give me the page number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: It is 6099. Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Right. I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And as I was saying to you, the first page shows a chart. He has list of negatives 1 to 10 on the left-hand side column, and he has titles to go with each of the negatives on the right-hand column?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You've never seen this, have you?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I don't think so. If -- I don't recall seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But is it possible that this was given to a member of your team?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, yeah. This guy was a professional photographer, so this would be part of his normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could you keep your voice up for me. And was he the only photographer that you employed for the purposes of taking the photographs of the crime scene during these two days?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: As -- as I recall, quite possibly. We did have a couple of black and white pictures that we developed locally, but they weren't submitted as part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But Mr. Pettersen was engaged for the purposes of?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Taking photographs of the crime scenes and the remains; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to have a look at a number of photographs if you will. I'll just get the page number. If you would look at 06116 in the same booklet. And starting with the first photograph, ERN number 00357616, which is 130 on e-court, could you tell me if you recognise what is depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Okay. This one's --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You have it. First photograph.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Okay. It was partly taken off there. 616 was the last three?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The exhibit, Mr. Draper, is 6116, and the first photograph has 00357616.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. Yeah. I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: This looks like a scene --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You'll have to keep your voice up. I'm finding it hard to hear you.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: This is scene 1. The three ladies that are in the trap door, you can't see them very good in this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you turn to the next photograph which is 00357599.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
