utterances.text: And please keep your voice up, Mr. Draper. The e-court number is 113. Do you recognise what's in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Okay. This is photo, a close-up picture of the three women that were in the trap door at the -- scene 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: When you say trap door, what do you mean by the trap door?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: The trap door that you had seen flipped up there beside the one woman, leading into the -- or root cellar or whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You mentioned finding -- you mentioned your team finding three bodies in a basement. Are these the three bodies?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: These are the three bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Would you look at the following photograph, 00357539, e-court 107. Is this another shot of that?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That's correct, another shot. Another close-up shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The following photograph, 00357624, e-court 139 -- 138?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Close-up of the lady on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is this a close-up of the lady on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Next photograph is 00357618.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: E-court 132. Do you recognise what that is depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Stove.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know where this was?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Quite frankly, I can't recall. It rings a bell but I can't exactly place it, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay. We'll move on. The next photograph is 000357489. And e-court number is 3. Can you tell us what is depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That -- you can just make out the charred remains of the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Are you in a position to say which body it is?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I don't want to say for sure, but it's one of the bodies at Stupni Do. I just can't pinpoint this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Would you look at the next photograph, 00357495, e-court 9.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: The same thing. You can --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Again is this another charred --

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Another charred body.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: -- photograph, charred body. Looking at photograph 00357966.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Be a --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Which is 7966 on e-court?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: It would be a photo of the mayor's dad, the one, the gentleman found near -- yeah, kind of in the woods a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The following photograph 0358238, which is --

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Of the same gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: -- 238 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah, that would be the same gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the next photograph, 00357965?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Close-up of his face, yeah. Same guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And that was 7965 on e-court. We then come to photograph 00357764.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Right. A view of the village in that location there at Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: This depicts the destruction?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And that was e-court number 278. That brings us on to photograph 7726, e-court 240. Is this another picture of the destruction?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Photograph 00357525, 39 on e-court. Is this another picture of the destruction?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: 7525. Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Then moving on to photograph 00357527, which is 41 on e-court. What have you depicted here?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: This is the scene 2 area there of the gentleman that at first we didn't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm still finding it hard to hear. Could you please keep your voice up?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: This gentleman has had his clothes burnt off except for his combat boots, as you can see the ... We assumed that he was a BiH defender. At first we weren't too sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: We move on to 00357522, e-court 36. Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Right. This is a -- the same gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Then turning to the next photograph, 00357519.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Same gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And I'll just find the e-court number for that. The e-court number is 33. Photograph 00358155, e-court 8155. What have we depicted in this shot?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: One of the charred corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The next photograph is photograph 00358153, e-court 8153. Again, is that one of the charred corpses?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the next photograph, number 00358092.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: One of the charred corpse.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: One of the charred corpses.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the e-court number on that is 8092. This brings us to 00357508. E-court 22. Again we have pictures of the charred corpses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. 7508, you said?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The next photograph is 00357498, e-court 12. Again we have charged corpses?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: On this occasion a charred corpse?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, one.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Charred corpse.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: E-court 27. Similar charred corpse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to save a minute or two, my learned friend for following the formal procedure needs to go through all these photographs in order to tender them, but I'm sure that all the photographs that are on the proofing chart, and I'm confident I can speak on behalf of all the Defence teams, even if they're not shown to the witness but are contained in the binder are quite acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I do propose tendering all of these photographs at the conclusion of this interview -- at the conclusion of this examination, Your Honour. Do you wish me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but is it necessary to see them all?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: It was for the record, but given the fact that I will be submitting a final table of exhibits with these photographs, I think -- and the fact that my colleagues on the Defence don't appear to have any objections and, for the sake of time, I don't think it's necessary to go through the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but there is a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I'd like to ask a question of the witness to have things clarified regarding photograph 00357599. We saw a person, I believe a lady, wearing a military uniform. Is the fact that she wears a military uniform, does it have anything to say as to whether she was a combatant or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I see the photo? I think this is one of the woman in the trapdoor, is it, on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. Quite.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. On occasion you see people wearing the tops of camouflage uniforms. I think if -- I believe that maybe if you saw a photo of her in the autopsy she may not have been wearing only the top, but from later witness interviews she -- she was -- she wasn't a member of an attacking -- or the defenders. She was with these ladies, huddled. This was a shelter area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Would you happen to know what age this lady was? Would that be a fair question to ask you? Do you remember? If you don't, just say so.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I'm not too sure. Around 26. I think the lady in the middle was the older lady and the other two were about the same age, younger.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: See -- these photographs which I've just shown you, did you see these photographs before?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your evidence this morning you've given evidence regarding Stupni Do, what you learned about the attack and the fact it was the HVO from Kiseljak commanded by Ivica Rajic, and you described having been told by various witnesses of pretty horrendous crimes committed against the inhabitants and villagers of the -- of the village, and you also told us that you prepared a number of reports. Do you know where your reports were sent ultimately?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: When they left my office they went to the command provost marshall at BH command Kiseljak, and from there they went to the force provost provo marshall who was based in Zagreb, and they would distribute them as they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Would they have eventually reached the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Are you aware on the 11th of February, 1994, the Secretary-General issued a special report dealing solely with the massacre in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'd like you to take a look at Exhibit 78 -- 07838 in your booklet, please.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Under -- under what tab?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Definitely never seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, could I ask you to turn to the second page and paragraph 6. Paragraph 6 states basically that -- that between the hours of 8.00 a.m. And 8.10 in the morning on the 23rd of October, 1993, while the village defence force was changing shifts effectively that the village came under attack, that the BiH armija force in Stupni Do congregated and that H [sic] forces began to attack the BiH forces in this area, eventually moving away at 1630 hours. At paragraph 7 the report quotes from UNPROFOR Nordic battalion sources about what happened afterwards, how they were prevented from going into Stupni Do. At paragraph 8, again reference is made to the UNPROFOR forces entering Stupni Do, finding the village having been burnt, 52 houses in the village showed signs of being burnt or burning. Fourteen bodies were discovered. Some were identified, some were not identified. On paragraph 9 it makes reference to the investigation of the events surrounding Stupni Do. At paragraph 10 it describes what many of the witnesses related to the investigators. At paragraph 11 it refers to the fact that some survivors from the attacks stated they had been raped. Number -- paragraph 12 deals with the manner in which they were interviewed. Is what I've just said to you being a synopsis of the report, is this the way your investigation took place and is this the information you learned during your course of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, it is, although I don't -- I do notice a few things. Like in paragraph 9, military police interviewed most of the 193 survivors of the attack, which is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: But basically, yes, generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, I know you haven't seen the report but the report effectively summarises your work, what happened in Stupni Do, your work, the work undertaken by your team members, and what left -- and what was left to be done; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you remember that you prepared a list of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- that's really just not correct. The witness has already drawn attention to one complete inaccuracy in the report and for Mr. Flynn to draw that sweeping conclusion that this document that this witness has never seen before effectively summarises his work is just not correct and in my submission it's no basis for the document to be admitted. It should be presented through a witness who knows about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we just support that and add that when Mr. Flynn said, "Is this the information you learned during the course of your investigation?", there is a danger that that sweepingly includes all the contents of the paragraphs which Mr. Flynn read out understandably quite hurriedly which, again, Mr. Murphy has emphasised the witness has never seen before. We need to be terribly careful about the limits of what this witness can actually say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Draper -- in answer do that, Mr. Draper, in paragraph 10 of the report on the third page, it says: "In describing the incident, many witnesses stated that the HVO attackers were wearing black uniforms with white bands on the left shoulder."

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: "And green camouflage uniforms."

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: "Some had camouflage faces and HVO patches.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: "While others had no identifying marks."

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: "While wearing black uniforms they also wore black baseball caps."

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: "And were suspected to be members of the HVO death squad or special forces from Kiseljak."

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: "One survivor believed that HVO from Vares and the Bobovac Brigade from Kiseljak took revenge on Stupni Do as a reprisal for BiH army offences --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- this -- I'm sorry to interrupt. This is completely improper. This witness has no personal knowledge whatsoever. I mean, his whole testimony has consisted of what he was told by other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: He wasn't able to see any of these events himself or conduct any investigation except to talk to others, and for him to be asked to verify these opinions and speculate on this report is completely incorrect. The Prosecution should call the proper witness if they wish to have this document admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, there are two reports, report 8021 dated 26th of March, 1994. That's the witness's report. He signed it. We can see his name in the report. And then there is a second report, 7838, sent to the Security Council on the 10th of February, 1994. The latter contains 13 paragraphs. To avoid any problem, if you want to emphasise the report sent to the Security Council, you have to ask the witness whether, based on his own report, which parts he drew from his own report, and you compare those portions to the report spent to the Security Council to see whether it's matching or whether there are inconsistencies. Otherwise, as pointed out by Mr. Stewart and Mr. Murphy, if you deal with the Security Council report and he, the witness, did not draft it, it was drafted by somebody else, it could be that there would be differences between the witnesses report and that other report. I mean it is, I think, a technical question of how to put the questions. You can solve the problem without causing objections. And I remind you that you can file your objections in writing. So, Mr. Flynn, if you ask those questions, you plan to insist on some salient points. Based on the witness's report, put the questions, and then you can say, "Well, you stated this, and in the Security Council report this is being said. So does this confirm your own conclusions, Witness, or is it different from your conclusions?"

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: That is what I was attempting to do. The witness hasn't seen the report before, and certainly we don't have time to go through the entire report, so I was trying to be selective, and I started with paragraph 10, and I was reading the contents of that report with the intention to say, "Was that your recollection? Was that the information gathered by you?" But he actually said as I was reading it, "I remember this. That is correct." And it was then that my colleague in the Defence objected. That was my intention, Your Honour, to take selective portions of the report and ask him to -- to inquire from him whether it corresponded with the testimony, information which he had been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed. Anyway, the Judges will have both reports, and we can draw some conclusions from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Exactly. And time won't allow me to question the witness about everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'll just ask you very briefly. At paragraph 11 of the report it is -- is it suggested that several female survivors from Stupni Do stated they had been raped by HVO soldiers during the attack. Others reported being robbed of their valuables, and in one case a 54-year-old grandfather had been killed by automatic machine-gun fire. Did you receive any information corresponding from that during the course of your investigations?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. As you're going over this, in my mind from the interviews I did I could relate to what was said in the interviews that were conducted and the information I had received and, yes, they do relate to information I received from the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And finally at paragraph 12, halfway down, it says: "The main suspects for the commission of these crimes appear to be extremist elements of the Croatian Defence Council from Kiseljak, Travnik, and Kakanj under the command of Ivica Rajic." Was that the information which you received and which you mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, earlier you -- you identified a list of deceased from Exhibit 08121, which you had prepared for us. I wonder could you go to your booklet and open that page for us, please. It's page R0048852 from Exhibit 8121. It's the list of deceased.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Right. I have it, Annex A.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you told us how you prepared that list earlier this morning.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, in addition to preparing that list did you see death certificates for any of the deceased?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: We received death certificate, burial permission slips that I obtained from the official from Dabravine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: And I attached them to an annex in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you compare the contents of those death certificates with the information which is on your list of deceased and did they match?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah. They -- I think there was maybe a date of birth off here or there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: But for the most part --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Would you leave that page open, please, for me. And I wonder if we could ask to be put up on e-court Exhibit number 8654. Do you have it in front of you, if you look at your screen? If you look at the television screen in front of you, do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: This is a death certificate in the name of Abdulah Likic, date of birth 31st of August, 1936, and if you look at the bottom of the page, the father's name is Likic Ibro. It was issued by the BiH authorities in 1996.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That's correct. I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could you go back to your list now and tell me if the same -- you have the same details?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Number 8 on the list there, Abdulah Likic, Ibro.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And date of birth?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: 31 August 1936.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the father's name?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Ibro.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Ibro. Now, I don't propose to bring you through all of the death certificates. Do you remember yesterday we did the same exercise in respect to many of -- all of the deceased on your list?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And apart from some minor discrepancies attributable either to some typos or dates being out by either one day or year, did the data correspond with the death -- did the data from your list correspond with the data which was on the death certificates, in particular the father's or mother's name?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Pretty well so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Have you any reason to believe that the certificates contained in Exhibit 08655, Exhibit 0867 [sic], Exhibit 08664, Exhibit 08684, Exhibit 08685, Exhibit 08687, Exhibit 08688, Exhibit 08691, and Exhibit 08692, have you any reason to believe that the certificates referable to those persons are any different to the persons mentioned in your death list?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I believe the ones that we went through there were put against the Annex A here. This exhibit pretty well matched up other than the typos and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, when you gathered all of the evidence during the course of your investigations, can you tell us what happened to it?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: All the evidence obtained during the course of the investigation was turned over to our evidence custodian that was Sergeant Lunge of Canadian nationality. He was the overall evidence custodian of the MP platoon. So the -- for example, the -- all the evidence that Staff Sergeant Verne had collected at the scene at Stupni Do would have been turned over at the first opportunity to Sergeant Lunge who would have taken control of it until it was handed over to, I think, the Hague here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And finally you mentioned earlier what efforts you had made to try and contact Ivica Rajic, and I think you mentioned that you had received information that he had left -- left Kiseljak. Did you receive any other information concerning Rajic from any source?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: One person I interviewed from which I determined that he had a name change was Xray in my last report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Who was Xray?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Xray.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Person --

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Xray was a person that we -- that was arrested and held at Kiseljak. And then eventually when I interviewed him he knew Rajic and had dealt with him. And at one point I was given a form that was instead of being signed by Rajic was now signed by -- and the name just escapes me right now. Can I --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you -- did you mention this in your report of the 26th of March, 1994?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Of the name change?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I don't think ... I have it in my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Okay, yeah. Yeah. On my last report there. I had mentioned two separate sources that indicate that he had changed his name to Viktor Andric.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Viktor?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Andric, A-n-d-r-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: One I think was in dispatch -- dispatches maybe that I had seen and the other was the interview I did with this person in the report was identified as Xray.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And this document that you -- that Xray handed you, did you see the name Andric on this document?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did Xray connect this document to Ivica Rajic?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I just want to refer to my notebook here. I think I have it written down there what document it was. Because I visually remember seeing it, but now, you know, I don't want to -- I'm not a hundred per cent sure memory-wise. I'll just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: This is my last question, Your Honours. I'll be finished after this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. This individual was -- on being released they were provided with charges which were being brought against them. A copy was received, yeah, but they did not know yet when they wanted to be -- they were going to be tried on the charges. They were ordered to report once a day to the military security personnel. This order was signed by Viktor Adric, A-d-r-i-c, [sic] which was Commander Redic or Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Commander Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You mention two sources. Did you hear this from another source?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: The other source, if I recall, it was probably on something like a sitrep documentation. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is this an UNPROFOR document?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah, it would have been an UNPROFOR document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I don't have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you, Mr. Flynn. Who is going to start for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions for the witness, and we have offered General Praljak any time that he may need that's available to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For your information, only the Defence teams for Mr. Petkovic and Praljak wish to use the available time also from the other Defence teams for our cross-examination. Following my examination, Mr. Praljak will put several questions to the witness himself. Could the usher please collect some documentation we have?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Draper. My name is Bozidar Kovacic, and I am counsel for one of the accused, General Praljak. I will have several questions for you. First, a question which has to do with some of your today's testimony, namely page 35, line 10 or around line 10 of today's transcript. Today you said that you sent a request, a query, through the UN structure up the structure where you sought assistance in getting in touch with HVO with a view to interviewing the participants in the action at Stupni Do. Do you recall testifying to that effect today?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In connection with this, did you again from the higher-up structures down to you receive any response in terms of what the HVO position was with regard to this request of yours? Did you -- did you receive any feedback as to whether the HVO had anything to do with the fact that you didn't receive any response? You said today that you didn't receive any feedback. The information you got, was it to the effect that they got in touch with the HVO but never got an answer from them, or you simply did not receive any response from your superior structure?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: If -- okay, if I can clarify. As a military policeman, what I was after was to interview people involved in the attack which I was never able to do. I did get feedback from the BH command legal. I believe his last name was Koet, K-o-e-t, and he had -- I think there was two letters that we got from him outlining his attempts and the results of communicating with the HVO. I remember seeing two memos from him, an initial one. I think it was with the HVO liaison officer, Lukic, or -- and with a Mr. Banik [phoen], if memory serves. And it -- it had dealt with information about the attack from the HVO side of the house. I remember on -- I remember reading in one that they had -- they had confirmed that Zijad Radic [phoen] was the senior member for the attack and there were two members of the attacking force that were shooting at civilians, if I recall correctly, but I was not able to -- they weren't available to be interviewed. I remember seeing these two memos. I do believe I attached it to one of my reports, did I not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us not go into any details concerning documents. Based on what you've just explained to us now, can we conclude that the HVO, through the contacts with UNPROFOR and the UN command, reacted positively and furnished at least some information relevant for the investigation at the time? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Would I say by providing the name of Rajic saying that he was the HVO commander and that the fact that there was two individuals that they had -- were shooting at civilians was, and that's why I think I attached them to the report. Notwithstanding that, it -- it wasn't my basic request from the memo that I had submitted, which was what I was after. It was to interview people. But there was communication definitely on a higher-up scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Except for the two memos you mention, you have no knowledge as to any further contacts between the UN command and the corresponding HVO commands concerning this event; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: No. That would have been way over my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us clarify the following: In your statements, including the statement you gave earlier and the reports, it is quite evident that whilst you were investigating the events at Stupni Do, you were aware of the fact that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was also conducting an investigation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: The BiH were doing an investigation on Stupni Do, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I believe that's right, because some of my witnesses were saying statements to BiH officials. That was one of the reasons why whenever we interviewed a witness we had to make sure that what they said to us was voluntary and not anything that they were told to say to us. We made that clear at the -- at each interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of course throughout this process it was quite clear to you that the BH army was also conducting an investigation and that they had some knowledge of these events. You confirmed this. Did the army provide you with any information concerning the results of their investigation, or did they at least give you some significant information relevant to the investigation you conducted?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Unfortunately a lot of times the people I was talking to, you know, I wouldn't know exactly who they were or -- unless it was written in my report, but if I could get -- find out where survivors were by talking to these officials and they led me to these Stupni Do villagers, I would have taken that information and used it. The gentleman I spoke to at Dabravine, he was, I'm sure, the official I got the list of deceased from, and the list of living. And I don't know whether he was a military or civilian, to be truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. As far as you know, you didn't receive, or at least you personally and your team, any final results of the investigation conducted by the BH army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: No. At one time I was trying to get reports from them, but BiH wouldn't give it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to the investigation or the steps taken by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown Exhibit 06091?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Or, rather, Mr. Witness, you have the folder in front you. Could you please look at the first document there. I will have questions for you concerning this document. And could you please read it. It consists of only two or three sentences. Let us first look at the date. It was written on the 25th of October and signed by Zarko Tole. We see his function written here. He was the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Okay. We're looking at 363, the last three digits? Is that the one you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. No. Oh, yes, yes. That's right. That's the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: That's the page of the -- that's the number of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From this document it follows that the chief of the Main Staff sent a letter on the 25th of October to the commander in Vares asking for accurate information concerning the events in the village of Stupni Do to be delivered. In the next sentence we can see that he already has some information because the commander of the Norwegian battalion stated that the fate of 200 civilians was unknown. "Submit detailed information on what happened in Stupni Do." Based on what you knew from before about the HVO conduct and investigation based on the contacts you had higher up, doesn't this letter show that the Main Staff reacted by seeking additional information from their own units in order to take any further action if need be? Do you agree with me that this request has to do with the events we're discussing?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: You're -- like the document I've never seen, so you just want me to look at this document and -- and say this is -- this is a true document? Because I don't have any knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. No. Let this be clear. I quite understand that you have probably not seen the document ever, and I'm absolutely not asking you to confirm the authenticity of this document, because you can have no knowledge of that. My question for you is: In view of the fact that you were involved in the investigation on Stupni Do, and in view of the fact that you had information about the HVO actions since your command had contacts with the HVO earlier on that we referred to, would you agree with me that when you read this letter, on face value it shows that the HVO was taking steps to get more information about these events, because the Main Staff, which was not stationed in Vares, sought information about the events that were the subject of your investigation? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Okay. So I understand that. Like you're doing your part of the investigation, you're trying to find out what happened to -- and that's what this reflects. And I can understand that, that you'd be going after that information yourself. As the BiH were going after the same information from their people, you would be going after that information from your people too. Yeah, I guess that's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct. Does it not appear that this letter has to do with these very events in Stupni Do, because the letter refers to events in Stupni Do? Does it not also show that the Main Staff, too, did not have any information about what had actually transpired at Stupni Do, because the information flow was poor, the communications were poor? Does this not show that the HVO was taking steps to obtain information on this? Would you not agree with what I'm saying? You had occasion to see HVO documents.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I guess, yeah. They were getting -- trying to get information on the Stupni Do incident from what I gather at this letter. And whether they knew what happened at Stupni Do or if they didn't know what happen at Stupni Do, I can't tell you that, but just by the appearance the letter they were going after information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of course you can't tell that. Thank you. In your statement you also said that on the first day you went to Stupni Do with your team in order to take the first steps in your investigation. Shortly after you, and you even said that you were in a hurry because with you there were some news crews who wanted to enter the village and film it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes. We --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You need not go into any details. There were foreign news crews that entered the village, is that right?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, once we were able to pass the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of course. And roughly speaking, the news crews entered the village several hours after you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: No. They were in the convoy with me. What happened is, once we got through the HVO check-point we went to the village and everyone parked in the field, and General Ramsay did an interview for the press people, and I was talking to the BritBat commander there. Then once I told him what we wanted to do, I had the BritBat commander, I think Hunter -- Roy Hunter, lead the way and the press people were coming behind us, and that's how it took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the journalists went in, right, with you. I didn't know that. But undoubtedly the cameramen filmed a lot of footage there that was then transmitted throughout the world through their respective systems; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at another document in the folder I provided you with. This is P 06104. It's a handwritten document, and you have the English translation of it. It's also very short. It was written in the forward command post at Citluk and addressed and sent to Vares. It was signed by the chief of the Main Staff. It's a very brief request wherein he says: "We have received a confirmation by the HTV," and HTV is the Croatian national television, "that they have footage of the massacre in Stupni Do which they had received through exchange with foreign agencies. "In order to take a correct stance, I'm demanding the truth about this event so that the HVO Main Staff may take the proper position." Would you agree that evidently the Main Staff learnt also on -- from the public television broadcaster that something had happen at Stupni Do because the HTV, the Croatian national television, broadcast footage at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. I know that the question appears innocuous, but I don't think he can assume what the Main Staff in Mostar saw or what they did not saw -- see. The letter suggests that they had confirmation that the Croatian TV had footage, but there is no indication that the Main Staff saw it. So perhaps it might be possible to rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I partly agree with the objection. The fact of the matter is, however, that the witness confirmed that television crews entered the village at the same time he did. The fact of the matter is that the news reached Europe very quickly, and it transpires from the first sentence of this document that the HTV confirmed possession of the footage on the massacre to the chief of the Main Staff, and the HTV could not possibly have received the footage from anyone else but the news crews that were there on the ground. I believe Their Honours are aware of the fact that news agencies exchange footage and news in the matter of minutes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] For your information, Your Honours, the first news from Stupni Do did not reach the world on the 27th when the news crews -- these news crews went down there. The BBC was there even before. Thus the 27th of October footage was not the first one to reach the world. I believe the first footage dated from the 26th or even earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think we need to prove the fact that the news was transmitted, because we have the witness saying now that he was there with the journalists at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, with respect to the objection raised by the Prosecution, apparently, but you've acknowledged it yourself, apparently the witness is not in a position to give us any assessment about the position taken by the Main Staff. So please rephrase your question. We have to remember that what's important in this handwritten document is the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may add a point. This paper here is dated October 25 the witness came to Stupni Do on October 27. How can the victim say anything about something that happened before he'd even been there? You will probably have a good explanation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have an explanation, and General Praljak provided part of it. The footage filmed by the journalists who were there on the same day as the witness, on the 27th, was not the first footage to be actually transmitted worldwide. It was, rather, on the 25th that we had -- as a result of the exchange of news agencies -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] No, no. There was no footage on the 25th. There was a radio report on that. I believe that this has to be clarified when we're talking about who reported or informed whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to come to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It is also a bit difficult to understand who is interrogating and examining whom right now. Does Mr. Praljak cross-examine Mr. Kovacic or -- because you seem to be in contradiction there, and it is a bit confusing for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, I believe that evidently General Praljak wanted to assist me by providing additional information that I may have overlooked. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Honourable Judge Trechsel, even if there were 50 lawyers in the courtroom they would not be able to reach an agreement about all the information we have. They would have to actually spend 24 hours a day together. I would have to give him my brain in order to be clear on all the points. I merely wanted to clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not be going back to this document. There is this one piece of information relevant with relation to the document, and it is up to Their Honours to decide whether the document should be in evidence or not. We have other ways of introducing this document into evidence. It is up to you, Your Honours. I believe it was important for the witness to comment on this document just as he commented on other documents that he never saw, like, for instance, the UN document he was shown among the last documents that he commented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I have a question for you, not regarding this document but the one before signed by Mr. Tole. I'm curious because of the heading of this document. I can see, "Union of the Republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Herceg-Bosna." I can't remember seeing this type of heading before, so what is that, this union of republics?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your -- President, if I can remind you, that's the time when the name Community Herceg-Bosna was changed into Republic of Herceg-Bosna. That had to do with international negotiations going on at the time, and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna used the terminology that cropped up at those negotiations. Sometimes there are inconsistencies that we believe are mainly due to translations produced during those negotiations. You will find several documents dating from October of that year where this term "Union" is used next to Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna on a par. I hope that I have explained this sufficiently for the time being, and maybe we will be able to clarify it further through other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to spend some more time on your second report of the 22nd March. For the record, it's P 08121. Without going into too many details, on page 1, item 1, you enumerated the names of certain direct perpetrators as you were able to collect them through the various interviews that you told us about. Do you know whether this report, or at least some information contained therein, had been conveyed to the HVO through contacts at your level or maybe at a higher level?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, the interpreter was -- you were coming through talking more than the interpreter was, but I think you were saying that the -- my reports went to HVO officials. Do I know if that happened? No, I don't know if that happened, sir. That wouldn't have been up to me. If such a thing happened, it would have been over my head. Once the report left me, it went to BH authorities, and they would decide who gets the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. While we're there, let us clarify one more point that was mentioned today. Based on your interviews with the victims, I'd like to ask you the following: Do you agree, and is it correct, that the participants in that event, the alleged perpetrators of crimes, would come or had come, according to interviewees, from Kiseljak? That was one place mentioned by the interviewees as the origin of the perpetrators. Some of them at least.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The next place mentioned was Kakanj. Some perpetrators seemed to have come from Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah, I believe that was one of the places mentioned too. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. And the next place mentioned was Mir village, not far from Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Some interviewees mentioned men from Vares.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you by any chance remember some details about the men from Vares? Were they supposed to be from Vares town or the broader area of the municipality of Vares?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I don't know if they were from the town or the broader an area. Only that the witnesses were able to just -- I don't know if the ones were from Vares, but some of them recognised their names or their voices because they were employed with them or went to school with them earlier in life. There was like a personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more thing in conclusion. You described to us the whole process of your work, the distribution of the workload, the crew that you had, the resources that you disposed of, and from all that it was clear that you were under a number of constraints. The situation was far from ideal. But it's obvious that you did undertake everything within your power to do that job in the best possible way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: That's the way that we're trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's right. In view of the number of the victims and the circumstances under which the crime occurred, you as a military -- as an experienced military policeman, would you say that if this investigation were conducted under normal circumstances in your country that the method of work, the number of people engaged, the resources used would be significantly better, including appropriate forensic experts, medical officers, the site visit would have lasted a lot longer? Could you just in a few words tell us about this comparison or possible differences between the way it would have been done in your country and the way it was actually done there?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I guess the easiest way to explain is there is -- the MP platoon over there, we didn't have no resources whatsoever nor -- no criminal investigation kit, no video cameras, no tape recorders, no cameras, no nothing. Everything that we used we obtained by ourselves not through -- like the video cameras weren't from the UN or any other detachment. We obtained them from -- for example, we obtained them from CanBat 2 in Visoko. It wasn't part of their military. It was -- these cameras were set up for use by soldiers to film themselves to send home videos. So I had two of my people go over and sign them up -- sign them out and we used them for the rest of our tour. We kept them signed out. We didn't have no equipment. Whereas in Canada you would have had complete criminal -- a team just set up for forensics, I imagine, all the resources, I guess, a big city would have. I don't know much about that to be truthful, but I imagine if the equipment is at a police officer's disposal he should be able to use it. So it was night and day if that's what you're getting at, between the resources available to us in, you know, Canada, say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the most critical link in that chain was the absence of post-mortems and the lack of autopsy reports and other expertise that results from post-mortems? Did you as an investigator feel that there is no compensating for this lack -- for this lacking component in any way that would be remotely appropriate? The footage filmed by the cameras intended for home videos did not remotely make up for that. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: If what you're saying is the -- the equipment that we didn't have or anything, none of that really mattered to me. The only thing that I was after was interviews with witnesses. And the more the merrier. That way you get cooperation. So as long as I got those interviews I wasn't too concerned about the rest of the information, you know, the evidence and that type of thing. What I needed was people that had first-hand knowledge of what had happened there, and the more cooperation I got, then the better. So just because we didn't have the equipment wasn't vital in my mind. What was vital was to get people who -- who were harmed, their statements, their interviews done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. We have to make a break because the tape is running out. We are going to have a 20-minute break and we will start, therefore, if 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resume. Before I give the floor back Mr. Kovacic, the registrar has to give some clarifications on an IC number. We might forget if we don't do it now. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Just one very quick clarification for the transcript and the record. Today we -- I have assigned an IC number, 513, to the list submit the by 5D for Witness Patrick van der Weijden. The -- in fact, the list was already in evidence under the Exhibit number IC 387. Therefore, the IC 513 exhibit is still available for the next list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for your information I just have one more question. I believe Mr. Praljak has several more, and then my colleague, Ms. Alaburic, will take over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, I have just one more question concerning your last answer. Would you agree that in a professional police investigation of any police force in the world material, forensic evidence, is more important than witness statements, than witness testimony?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Before we answer that, could I just go back to a question that you had asked previously? I don't want to mislead you. And that was when you asked about the soldiers from Vares, and I might have given you an impression that there was lots of soldiers from -- HVO soldiers from Vares that took place in the attack, and I racked my brain while we had the break, and I definitely can say they were from Mir. But as for Vares, I remember one person saying that he worked with a guy that worked in the mine at Vares-Majdan or like that, something like that, but for the lie of me I can't recall, you know, a bunch of them or anything. In fact, when they are stranded out in the bush there when they came to the check-point the locals there had kind of helped them out. As for this last question, first-hand eyewitness evidence is, in my book, the best, especially when it is corroborated by other witnesses, and that supports all the forensic evidence, although I agree with you that DNA evidence is -- certainly puts people in certain places, and the same as fingerprints. So, you know, definitely useful. But when you have witnesses that give evidence, what could be more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Draper, I would like to put a question in this context. You have also not really answered another part of a question of Mr. Kovacic, Mr. Draper, and that was the question as to what defects does the investigation have due to the absence of a proper post-mortem and autopsies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It -- the absence would -- wouldn't give the exact cause of death. Is that what you're getting at? That I agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not talking in general terms. I'm talking about your investigation. Did it suffer? Does it show weaknesses due to the absence or the lateness of autopsy or post-mortem? I believe that was the question Mr. Kovacic had posed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It -- it would -- it would be better if the autopsies were done as soon as possible, if -- yeah, certainly. The same as all evidence. You know, if we were right there right at the -- the outset to get all the evidence and could account for it, that would be great too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But do you -- do you feel that this is a weakness of your report, that there must be -- one must read it with caution because in the case of this investigation there was no immediate post-mortem and autopsy but it was delayed, and maybe not up to the highest standards of forensic medicine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, it wouldn't be up to the highest standards of -- of that notwithstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, following up on the question put by Judge Trechsel, and I don't think my question is going to interfere at all with the cross-examination. Witness, I do have some knowledge in this field, and I was really struck, looking at the footage but also looking at the photographs, but especially at the video footage. I noted this: We saw some bodies, charred bodies spread out throughout the village at some places. I really watched closely where they were and what was around the bodies, and I asked myself this technical question, and I know you are a specialist so you might be able to answer my question: The bodies obviously were carbonised. They were burned. How? We don't know. However, on several occasions I saw that around the bodies there was no trace of flames, of fire, of anything burnt. You see the body, the charred body, and next to it there's no trace at all of fire or of flames. There could be three ways. There was a shell, incendiary shell that fell next to the body, or it could have been sprinkled with fuel and then burned, or you use a flame thrower. But at least in the last two hypotheses, the space around the body should show traces of fire or flames, of being burnt. And on several occasions on the video footage you can't see anything, so I asked myself, the bodies we saw, were they not transported on the location whilst they were burnt elsewhere? So hence the technical questions raised by Mr. Kovacic and my colleague. When you carried out your investigation, did you look into that question, namely how the bodies were burned and how it came that around the bodies there was no trace of flames or fire or incendiary material? Do you have a technical answer to provide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you had mentioned, you kind of indicated I was a specialist at the beginning of your statement, and I'm not whatsoever an expert in any of that type of thing. The bodies could have been moved there. They -- they -- it could -- any one of the scenarios you said. I don't know. I couldn't give you an explanation. Whereas through the interviews we had there were accounts of these people being dragged into the homes that were already on fire. So that's why the -- the eyewitness accounts were ever so important in this investigation. But forensic evidence would definitely, I assume, tell you how the bodies were burnt, if there were any accelerants used or that type of thing, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We won't go any more with this topic of the importance of forensics in investigations. Just one more thing. We saw, among other things, victims here that are bearing traces of one or two gunshot wounds, and it transpires from their autopsy reports, whatever their value, how they sustained them. If there is gunpowder on the wound, it could be established with the naked eye whether the person was shot point blank or from a greater distance, and that would help us establish whether the victim had been killed as a result of a conflict or executed at close range. Would you agree that it would have been good if we had such forensic data? Would you agree that such forensic evidence would be extremely welcome, bearing in mind all the evidence provided by the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sorry, we have little time. Would you just briefly answer with a yes or no, or maybe "I don't know," if you don't know, because we really don't have time for long explanations. Did I give you an example which shows that forensic evidence was important in this case, at least in some examples?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I'm quite sure you're right, sir. That's why the bodies were burnt, to get rid of the forensic evidence, if you know what I mean? If there was forensic evidence like gunpowder burns, you know by burning the bodies it kind of disappears. But for -- for the bodies that weren't burnt, yeah, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have more questions about this, but in view of the time constraints I'm going to let my client continue the examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Draper. I would appreciate short answers, and if you want to give a longer explanation, could you please indicate that to me. I took part in that war, and when we look at photographs like this we must understand that that's part of those things that war brings, and we have to face them. You said that from your information from various sources the village was defended by 36 members of the BH army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, approximately 36. That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. From your scouting of the village, did you observe any trenches around the village?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: We didn't go outside the village just due to safety concerns, for the team's safety itself. So, no, I didn't go through any trenches, sir. But through --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. Could you -- could you please answer again, because my -- my headset was turned off for a second. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll repeat my answer. No, we didn't go and visit any of the trench areas because of -- for safety concerns. It was a little bit too far out of the village, and we wouldn't be able to have the security provided with us, but I -- so to answer your question, I personally didn't, no. We were there, sir, if that's what you mean. Defenders said there were trenches as we were manning them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know based on the interviews that you made that during the HVO attack on that defended village whether shooting came from houses as well as trenches? Are you aware that houses also held some combat positions?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Quite possibly, because I know there was BiH defenders protecting the shelters where inhabitants were protected.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Similarly, you noted quite clearly that 193 persons from that village survived what we call the massacre at Stupni Do. Is that right, 193 persons left that village alive?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Quite possible -- yeah, right around that number. There might have been a few more that weren't on the list that I first received.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In your report on page 17 of the Croatian version, there's something I want to read and then you will comment. It says: "Most HVO members were horrified when they had heard what had happened at Stupni Do. Nobody had told them about it before. The soldiers brought some food and treated them kindly." This is a reference to the large group of refugees received at that HVO check-point. You say: "Two UNPROFOR vehicles arrived, but the HVO prevented them from being evacuated because they were afraid. They were fearing -- they were fearing a BH army attack." Is it true what you said in this report that these soldiers were horrified? One. And secondly, is it true that HVO soldiers received refugees at their check-point and later enabled them to cross over to BH-held territory?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah, I recall that. That was from some of the witnesses and that group of refugees that arrived at that check-point that was manned by local HVO, and they were, I recall from the interview, they were -- didn't really realise what had gone on, weren't aware of it and what happened, and they were shocked at the events, and I believed dressed some of the wounded and give them some bread and some -- along those lines, what they had.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On page 13 of your report you say that based on some information you received later you learnt of something that was found at Stupni Do, and it was a sign which had the letters HOS there and an emblem of a chequerboard, red and white squares, and beneath the sign it said, "For homeland ready." Have I quoted your words well?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yes, more than likely. I remember that was probably on the 12th of November, 1993, when we had a return trip to Stupni Do and we were trying to identify all the body locations and the names of those people, and it was found on the ground at that time. Is this the one -- I'm sure you read it. Is this the one where Master Corporal McKee says that it was quite noticeable and he would have noticed it last time around?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know that the HOS was not under the command of the Croatian Defence Council? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that these units were either an independent military force or are under the command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: From the information I gathered from interviews they were under the command of Colonel Ivica Rajic from Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I didn't receive interpretation. I'm not denying that they may have been under the command of Ivica Rajic, but they were not under the command of the HVO, but never mind. I should like to put another question to you, and could we have that video on standby, the one that we already watched. I would like it to be stopped at some sections. When on the 27th of October you entered the village for the first time, you inspected the village carefully and thoroughly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Not myself. I had Master Corporal Scott McKee do the crime scene processing so he would have gone through it very closely, whereas I did a general walkthrough of the village to see what was what. I myself did not go through each crime scene processing it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm interested in the following, Mr. Draper: Any one of the four TV crews, there were also security officers there, Mr. McKee, and you, all of you there were able to find 16 corpses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: Yeah. One of which that didn't appear to look like -- well, we didn't know if it was an animal or human. But we treated it as a human. And ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Fine. So there could have been less than 16, but you definitely found 16 corpses. Can you explain the Honourable Judges in what way you were able to find 22 more bodies at a later stage, thus arriving at the total number of 37? This remains an enigma, a mystery. If you entered the village, you inspected it thoroughly and photographed it and established that there were 16 bodies. In what way were you subsequently able to arrive at 37 persons who were killed at Stupni Do through whichever procedures you used? And I don't know which sort of procedures these could have been. How is this possible?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: After the 16 bodies were done and we left the area in early November, BiH authorities, I guess, mounted an offensive or whatever and took over the Stupni Do area. And once it was back under their control, the villagers were able to go back to their village, and of course the relatives and the victims knew where people were killed, and -- plus do a more thorough search for bodies, and that's where the rest were discovered, because while we were there we did not shift through any of the burnt-down houses. Most of the bodies were found underneath debris from buildings that had collapsed in on them. And as -- with the more interviews I did, the more corroboration I could get from people that had found these bodies. For example --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My apologies, sir. Excuse me. Could we now have that video clip shown, and we will see that there are quite a few burnt houses there, but there are no ruins there. We will stop at some sections, and you will tell me which ruins you were supposed to shift through or sift through to find these additional corpses. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could we have the video played?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, the video, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The first one. The long clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Which part of the first one are we talking about, the part with the bodies, the crime scenes, or are we talking about the part with the damage to the buildings? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Both of them. I will ask them to be stopped at some points to put questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, please let me know when you see the ruin that you were supposed to go through where you were unable to see dead bodies beforehand. We can see that the houses were burned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stop there. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is this a ruin?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: This is scene 1 where around -- so you're asked after the 22 bodies that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, please. I'm the one leading this. You're telling me that this is a ruin. We can't go into all the details, repeating that this is scene 1. You are here to assist us. You are supposed to say, "This is a ruin. We didn't have time to go through the ruin, and there may have been a dead body left beneath there." So please can you confirm for me the following: Is this a ruin?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I'm not quite following you. The -- I cannot tell you what houses or what ruins the rest of the bodies were in. Only the people that found the bodies can do that for you. I wasn't there when it happen. So how can I say what building they were in? I would just be guessing or assuming. I can point out on the map that I made out, but those buildings and how they relate to the ruins on this film, I never lived there before, so I won't be able to say exactly which ruin the bodies were recovered in. Only the people that lived there and found the bodies would be able to do that, I would think, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Draper. The military police of the UN international forces went into a village, the village we're dealing with here. You were investigating there until the month of March 1994. You sign a report. You're talking about, at first, 16 persons plus some additional corpses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I must ask you to keep to the facts. There is no way that this witness has been investigating from the moment he started on 27 October 1993 until the month of March 1994. He was not there from A to B. Maybe it's a difficulty of the translation, but it gives a wrong impression. He did not stay several months there, he told us. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Very well. Honourable Judge, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I apologise. But he was not in Stupni Do all the time. That is what I wanted to say. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I didn't say that. Can the basis be accepted? We have the fact that four TV crews and a group of international professional police investigators visited a village that was burned but was not in ruins, and one did not need to have excavators there. One could see dead bodies, both those burned and unburned, and then they established that there were 16 bodies. The rest is propaganda. This was used in the BH press, who increased the number up to 100, and here they increased it to 37. I'm not trying to downplay the events. I only wish to arrive at the truth of what actually happened and at the accurate figures. How could one get from the figure of 16 to 37? Where were 22 bodies then? We're not talking about possibly two bodies that they might have overlooked. These were 22 bodies that were additionally listed as Stupni Do victims.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's why, Mr. Draper, I'm asking you to indicate for me here where is that ruin which held so much rubble that you had to dig under there to find 22 persons? But I may move on. I will move on to other matters. Could we play the video.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could you stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Evidently we could see a woman on the right-hand side wearing a military shirt and a military jacket. Is that true, Mr. Draper? Is that what we were able to see there?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I can't tell from here -- from here, but, yeah, there was one that had a military top on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The third woman whose photograph we did not see, who was between the two women in the background, was she not also wearing a military jacket? You may know that or not. One of the two women we can see is wearing a military jacket. The other one isn't. What about the third woman who was killed there? Did she have a military uniform on or not? If you don't know, tell us, and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I'm not seeing anything on my screen other than black. Have you got a different. There was a flash of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can I suggest that rather than taking this video where one doesn't see anything, I didn't even distinguish a woman, you did back, Mr. Praljak, for your question to the pictures, and the picture 00357599 would be the good one, I suggest. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] 599. Yes, please. Could we please have photograph 00357599.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could we have the photograph? 6116.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The photograph Mr. Praljak is showing you to is 113. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] No. 7599. That's the photograph. Could you enlarge it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you see, sir, that the woman who was killed and who is on the right-hand side is wearing a T-shirt and a jacket that are part of a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: The vest definitely looks military. T-shirt, it looks kind of greenish, military greenish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Draper, you're saying "it seems." Let us be specific. Is this the top part of a military uniform, the T-shirt and the jacket? You're a professional officer?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: It looks like one, sir, but -- but maybe, yeah, it looks like one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. The woman whose had head we see leaning forward and who was killed there, was she wearing a military uniform or not, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NELSON DRAPER
utterances.text: I can't tell from this photo, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: As long as we have the picture, there is fabric with a kind of a flower pattern on the lower part of the woman to the right in the picture. Can you tell us what this is?
